candidate_sources.title: Maple Anthracnose : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Maple anthracnose symptoms include vein-associated lesions, discrete necrotic spots, and/or irregular necrotic blotches. Lesions have distinct margins and are located along leaf veins. On Japanese maple, lesions occur along primary veins and leaf margins and can appear both tan or black in color. The most important management strategy is sanitation: removing infected fallen leaves. Anthracnose is primarily an aesthetic concern and does not impact established trees.

candidate_sources.title: Maple (Acer spp.)-Anthracnose | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose of maple is caused by fungal pathogens including Aureobasidium apocryptum and Discula species. Symptoms include lesions along leaf veins and margins. Management includes sanitation, removing fallen leaves, avoiding overhead irrigation, and maintaining tree vigor.

candidate_sources.title: Common Disease Pests of Maple in North Carolina | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: On Japanese maples, anthracnose appears as creamy or tan-colored, angular blotches on the leaf margins and veins, with reddish-brown to light tan blotches. Anthracnose is caused by fungal pathogens such as Aureobasidium apocryptum, Discula campestris, and Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. In most cases the disease is cosmetic; in extreme infections defoliation and shoot dieback may occur. Spores overwinter on dead leaves and twigs.

candidate_sources.title: Aureobasidium apocryptum (Anthracnose on maple) - Bugwoodwiki
candidate_sources.snippet: Aureobasidium apocryptum (formerly Kabatiella apocrypta) is the causal fungus of anthracnose on maple. Describes pathogen biology, symptoms of vein-associated lesions and necrotic blotches, disease cycle, and overwintering on infected leaf litter and twigs.

candidate_sources.title: Phomopsis Canker : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Japanese maple (Acer palmatum) is one of the most frequently diseased trees in managed landscapes of southern New England, and Phomopsis sp. has been found in cankers at the node. Typical symptoms include thinning canopies, browning and prematurely shedding foliage, scattered branch dieback, and eruptive cankers on the bark. Management: prune cankered stems and branches at least 6â€“12 inches away from blighted tissue and remove diseased material.

candidate_sources.title: Phomopsis canker and twig blight (Michigan State University Extension)
candidate_sources.snippet: Phomopsis (syn. Diaporthe) causes cankers and twig blights on a wide range of woody ornamentals. The fungus infects plants through wounds from freezing, sunburn, drought, or pruning cuts, causing sunken lesions, branch dieback and twig blight. Pruning out infected tissue and reducing plant stress are key management practices.

candidate_sources.title: Maple (Acer spp.)-Branch Cankers | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Branch cankers of maple (Acer spp.) are caused by several fungi including Phomopsis spp., producing sunken lesions on shoots and branches, cracking and sloughing bark, and branch dieback. Management includes pruning infected branches and avoiding wounding and plant stress.

candidate_sources.title: Maple (Acer spp.)-Powdery Mildew | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Powdery mildew on maple caused by Sawadaea and Phyllactinia species. White fungal growth with small black fruiting bodies (chasmothecia) on undersides of mature leaves. Management: pick up and discard fallen leaves, deep water during drought, apply fungicides at 7- to 14-day intervals.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Sawadaea polyfida Causing Powdery Mildew of Acer palmatum in China | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Sawadaea polyfida occurs natively on Japanese maples (Acer palmatum) in China, Japan, and Korea. White powdery patches develop on leaves with chasmothecia. First report documenting the pathogen on A. palmatum.

candidate_sources.title: First record of Sawadaea polyfida causing powdery mildew on Acer palmatum and A. japonicum in Switzerland and Europe
candidate_sources.snippet: Sawadaea polyfida causing powdery mildew on Acer palmatum and A. japonicum. White fungal colonies on leaves with robust mycelial growth compared to Phyllactinia. First European record of the disease.
